To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

gay, lesbian, and heterosexual female therapists are rated more helpful by gay and lesbian participants than heterosexual male therapists, and the helpfulness of therapists is related to the extent to which they engage in negative and positive practices.

lesbian, gay, and bisexual therapists and female heterosexual therapists were more helpful than male heterosexual therapists, that therapist behaviors that were rated negatively were associated with ratings of unhelpfulness and termination, and that therapist behaviors that are rated positively are associated with ratings of helpfulness and with continuation in therapy.

gay, lesbian, and heterosexual female therapists of both genders are more helpful than heterosexual men, and that the practices that therapists employ are more predictive of helpfulness than are therapist demographics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between client ratings of therapist helpfulness and therapist practices.
the effects of therapist characteristics and practices on the perceived helpfulness of psychotherapy for gay and lesbian clients.
the effects of therapist sexual orientation, gender and practices on ratings of helpfulness by lesbian and gay clients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lesbian and gay clients prefer to work with lesbian or gay therapists of either gender or with heterosexual female therapists.

gay and lesbian therapists of both sexes, as well as heterosexual female therapists, were rated as more helpful than were heterosexual male therapists, and that the most helpful therapists engaged in positive counseling practices and avoided the negative practices.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most effective therapists are those who are gay, lesbian, or bisexual and who exhibit a positive and affirming style of counseling.

therapists who exhibit positive counseling practices and avoid negative counseling practices are more likely to be perceived by clients as helpful, regardless of therapist sexual orientation or gender.
gay and lesbian clients prefer therapists who are gay, lesbian, or bisexual and female.
The main takeaway from our work is that

therapists should be aware of how they might be perceived as helpful or unhelpful, and should strive to exhibit positive counseling practices. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
